Ruddy ground dove (Columbina talpacoti) females produce two eggs per clutch [N_R_i = two eggs per clutch], and field studies across their Neotropical range indicate they typically complete approximately 2.5 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 2.5 clutches per year], a reproductive frequency that is moderately high among small columbids. The incubation period for this species proceeds at a developmental temperature near 36 °C [T = 36 °C], and under these thermal conditions the eggs hatch after 12.5 days [ab = 12.5 days], a duration that aligns closely with predictions based on egg mass in small doves. Clutches are often initiated shortly after rain events, which likely synchronizes peak nestling demand with periods of elevated food availability. Both parents share incubation duties, an investment that permits nearly continuous thermal regulation of the developing embryos. The relatively short incubation period compared to larger members of the family Columbidae reflects the allometric scaling of developmental rates with adult body mass, a pattern well documented across avian lineages.

Newly hatched nestlings of the Ruddy ground dove emerge with a wet weight of approximately 3.5 grams [Wwb = approximately 3.5 grams], a very modest mass that is nevertheless sufficient to support the rapid growth trajectory characteristic of altricial doves. The initial wet weight of the freshly laid egg is 3.6 grams [Ww0 = 3.6 grams], indicating that the hatchling loses only a small fraction of its original mass during development, a consequence of efficient yolk-to-tissue conversion and minimal water loss through the porous eggshell. Upon reaching sexual maturity, individuals attain an ultimate wet weight of 36.3 grams [Wwi = 36.3 grams], representing nearly a tenfold increase from the neonatal mass. This pattern of exponential early growth followed by a plateau near the adult asymptotic mass is typical of small, rapidly maturing bird species. The substantial mass gain during the nestling period is supported by frequent parental provisioning of crop milk and seeds, a dietary shift that fuels the rapid deposition of both lean tissue and lipid reserves.

Under the sustained thermal conditions typical of active metabolic periods in this species, which average approximately 40.63 °C [T = 40.63 °C], the developmental milestones of young doves follow a predictable sequence. Fledging, defined as the age at which the chick achieves sustained flight and departs the nest, occurs at 9.5 days after hatching [tx = 9.5 days after hatching], an exceptionally brief nestling period even by columbid standards at a temperature of 40.63 °C [T = 40.63 °C]. This rapid exit from the nest likely serves as a hedge against high nest predation rates, which are considerable in their open-cup nesting habitats. Post-fledging care continues for an extended period, however, as the parents continue to provision the young. This combination of a short nestling phase and extended post-fledging dependence is a life-history strategy that balances the competing pressures of nest vulnerability and the need for adequate nutritional support during the final stages of somatic maturation. The thermal regime used in captive rearing studies closely mirrors the average body temperature of brooding adults.

Puberty in the Ruddy ground dove, marking the onset of gonadal maturation and reproductive competence, occurs at 28.5 days after hatching [tp = 28.5 days after hatching] when maintained at an ambient temperature of 40.63 °C [T = 40.63 °C], a value that reflects optimal captive rearing conditions. However, it is important to note that the onset of actual reproductive behavior, as distinct from physiological puberty, is substantially delayed. The time since birth at first brood is considerably longer, recorded at 140 days after hatching [tR = 140 days after hatching] at the same temperature regime. This temporal gap between the attainment of gonadal maturity and the first successful breeding attempt is common among small tropical doves and is thought to reflect the time required to acquire a territory, secure a mate, and gain the foraging experience necessary to sustain the energetic demands of egg production and parental care. Field observations corroborate this pattern, with first-year birds often participating in non-breeding flocks during their early months.

Longevity data for the Ruddy ground dove, derived from both captive records and mark-recapture studies in the wild, indicate a maximum lifespan of 12775 days [am = 12775 days] when individuals are maintained at a stable body temperature of 40.63 °C [T = 40.63 °C]. This translates to approximately 35 years, an exceptionally long lifespan for a bird of only 36 grams adult body mass, and one that places this species among the most long-lived of the small columbids. Such extended longevity is unusual for a rapidly reproducing, high-fecundity species and suggests that adult survival rates are remarkably high in the absence of intense predation pressure. The species' ability to persist for multiple decades likely reflects its generalist foraging habits, its use of stable secondary forest habitats, and a physiological capacity for sustained somatic maintenance. The combination of a very short fledging age with an extraordinarily long adult lifespan positions the Ruddy ground dove as an outlier within the typical fast-slow life-history continuum observed in small passerines and near-passerines, illustrating that small body size does not invariably predict a short total lifespan.
